title: Building Boolean Logic Circuits
summary: Following retrieval on 4-bit binary addition and single-gate rules, pupils complete a concise warm-up explaining how to trace intermediate wire states across four multi-gate circuit examples (supported by four dedicated empty placeholder slides for the teacher's circuit diagrams) to determine whether an output bulb is ON or OFF. The majority of the lesson is then dedicated to an extended hands-on workshop in an online Boolean circuit simulator, where pupils construct and test logic circuits to match completed target truth tables and copy each working circuit diagram into their books before advancing.

starterRetrievalFocus.q1LastLesson: Perform a 4-bit column-by-column binary addition with carry bits and state whether an overflow error occurs.
starterRetrievalFocus.q2LastWeek: Identify an AND gate from a diagram: provide an open-response prompt with dedicated space for the teacher to insert an AND gate image (not multiple choice).
starterRetrievalFocus.q3EarlierTopic: True or False check: Inputs A and B are both ON (1) for an OR gate—state whether the output is ON/True or OFF/False.
starterRetrievalFocus.q4Challenge: True or False check: Inputs A and B are both ON (1) for an AND gate—state whether the output is ON/True or OFF/False.

activeTaskTypes: 8 mins — Mini-whiteboard warm-up tracing intermediate wire states across 4 on-screen logic circuit examples to determine whether the bulb at the end is ON or OFF: include a short explanation slide followed by 4 empty placeholder slides for the teacher to insert the 4 logic circuit diagrams.

35 mins — Extended online Boolean circuit simulator workshop (per teacher brief exception): pupils are presented with completed target truth tables, construct and test a logic circuit in the online simulator to produce each truth table, and copy the working circuit diagram into their books before moving on to the next challenge.
pedagogicalRationale: Honours every teacher instruction and exception for Lesson 5 within the 60-minute budget (~8 mins retrieval starter, 8 mins circuit-tracing warm-up, 35 mins simulator workshop, ~9 mins buffer). Preserves the exact starter specifications (4-bit binary addition with overflow check, open-response AND gate identification with space for an inserted image rather than multiple choice, and True/False output checks when inputs A and B are both ON for OR and AND gates). Structures the 8-minute warm-up with a brief explanation of intermediate wire tracing (preventing mis-5) followed by 4 empty slides for the teacher's circuit diagrams before dedicating 35 minutes to building circuits from completed truth tables in the online simulator and recording each verified circuit in books.

slidesBlueprint.title: Starter
slidesBlueprint.contentSummary: Four-quadrant retrieval grid covering prior learning only: Q1 asks you to perform a 4-bit column-by-column binary addition (1011 + 0110) with a carry row and state whether a 4-bit overflow error occurs; Q2 gives an open-response prompt asking you to name the logic gate shown, with a dedicated blank space for the teacher to insert an AND gate diagram rather than multiple choice; Q3 asks True or False whether the output is ON (1) when inputs A and B are both ON (1) for an OR gate; Q4 asks True or False whether the output is ON (1) when inputs A and B are both ON (1) for an AND gate. Includes in-place one-by-one answer highlights.
slidesBlueprint.pupilActivity: Solve all four retrieval questions on your mini-whiteboard and self-mark as each quadrant answer highlights on screen.

pedagogicalRationale.cognitiveLoadNote: Activates prior schemas for 4-bit binary addition, overflow detection, and single-gate rules (AND, OR) in working memory before chaining multiple gates together.
pedagogicalRationale.retrievalLink: Retrieves 4-bit binary addition and overflow from Lesson 3 and AND/OR logic gate symbols and state rules from Lesson 4.

slidesBlueprint.title: Building Boolean Logic Circuits
slidesBlueprint.contentSummary: Clean, uncluttered lesson title slide displaying the title 'Building Boolean Logic Circuits', today's date, the guiding question 'How do you combine logic gates to control a final output?', and a visual illustration of interconnected logic gates feeding an output bulb.
slidesBlueprint.pupilActivity: Read today's lesson focus and prepare your book and mini-whiteboard for multi-gate circuit tracing.

pedagogicalRationale.principle: Cognitive Load Theory: Minimising Extraneous Load
pedagogicalRationale.cognitiveLoadNote: Keeps the title slide free of dense vocabulary definitions so pupils orient immediately to today's practical goal.
pedagogicalRationale.retrievalLink: Bridges from single logic gates in Lesson 4 to connected multi-gate circuits.

slidesBlueprint.title: What Is a Truth Table?
slidesBlueprint.contentSummary:
What Is a Truth Table?
• Imagine testing two switches in every position to see when a bulb lights up.
• A truth table lists every OFF (0) and ON (1) input with its output.
Key point: Each row shows one input combination and its exact output.

slidesBlueprint.title: How Truth Tables Work
slidesBlueprint.contentSummary:
How Truth Tables Work
• Step 1: List inputs in order from both OFF (0, 0) to both ON (1, 1).
• Step 2: Apply the gate rule to each row to record Output Q (0 or 1).
Remember: Two inputs always give four rows: 00, 01, 10, 11.

slidesBlueprint.title: Chaining Gates With Wires
slidesBlueprint.contentSummary: Hooks you with an everyday analogy: imagine a car engine starter that checks if the seatbelt is buckled AND the brake pedal is pressed, then passes that signal down an internal wire to a master switch before lighting the dashboard ready bulb. Explains that multi-gate circuits work the same way by passing a binary 0 or 1 along an intermediate wire from the output of Gate 1 into the input of Gate 2.
slidesBlueprint.pupilActivity: Follow how a binary signal travels out of the first gate along an internal wire before entering the second gate.

pedagogicalRationale.principle: Rosenshine Principle 2: Present New Material in Small Steps
pedagogicalRationale.cognitiveLoadNote: Grounds the abstract idea of an intermediate wire in a familiar two-stage physical switch system before showing circuit notation.
pedagogicalRationale.retrievalLink: Builds on single-gate input and output states from Lesson 4.

slidesBlueprint.title: Tracing Intermediate Wire States
slidesBlueprint.contentSummary: Models a three-step method for finding whether an output bulb at the end of a multi-gate circuit is ON (1) or OFF (0): Step 1, check the starting inputs (A = 1, B = 0) entering the first gate; Step 2, apply the first gate's rule and write the resulting 0 or 1 directly onto the intermediate wire P; Step 3, use wire P as the input to the final gate to decide if the output bulb is ON or OFF.
slidesBlueprint.pupilActivity: Follow the three-step worked trace from left to right and observe how writing the intermediate wire value prevents guessing mistakes.

pedagogicalRationale.principle: Rosenshine Principle 4: Provide Models and Worked Examples
pedagogicalRationale.cognitiveLoadNote: Externalises the intermediate wire state onto the diagram so pupils never hold multiple gate evaluations simultaneously in working memory (preventing mis-5).
pedagogicalRationale.retrievalLink: Applies Lesson 4 rules for NOT, AND, and OR gates sequentially.

slidesBlueprint.pupilActivity: Trace the intermediate wire state for Circuit Diagram 1 on your mini-whiteboard and write whether the output bulb is ON or OFF.

pedagogicalRationale.principle: Rosenshine Principle 3: Ask Questions and Check for Understanding
pedagogicalRationale.cognitiveLoadNote: Provides an uncluttered canvas for the teacher's first circuit diagram so pupils focus purely on tracing intermediate wires to the output bulb.
pedagogicalRationale.retrievalLink: Practises the left-to-right intermediate wire tracing method modelled on Slide 4.

slidesBlueprint.pupilActivity: Trace the intermediate wire state for Circuit Diagram 2 on your mini-whiteboard and write whether the output bulb is ON or OFF.

pedagogicalRationale.principle: Rosenshine Principle 6: Check for Student Understanding
pedagogicalRationale.cognitiveLoadNote: Completes the four-diagram warm-up sequence, allowing the teacher to confirm high success rates before transitioning to the simulator.
pedagogicalRationale.retrievalLink: Synthesises NOT, AND, and OR gate tracing across multi-stage wires.

slidesBlueprint.title: Spot the Wire Error
slidesBlueprint.contentSummary: Presents a Spot-the-Error diagnostic check targeting the misconception of skipping intermediate wires: Input A = 1 and Input B = 1 enter an AND gate, whose intermediate wire P feeds into a NOT gate before the bulb. Sam skips wire P and claims: 'Both inputs are 1, so the output bulb must be ON (1).' Is Sam right or wrong, and what is the state on wire P?
slidesBlueprint.pupilActivity: Write whether Sam is right or wrong on your mini-whiteboard along with the binary value on intermediate wire P.

pedagogicalRationale.principle: Rosenshine Principle 6: Check for Student Understanding (Hinge Point)
pedagogicalRationale.cognitiveLoadNote: Directly surfaces misconception mis-5 (guessing final outputs directly from initial inputs without recording the intermediate wire state).
pedagogicalRationale.retrievalLink: Combines AND gate and NOT gate inversion rules from Lesson 4.

slidesBlueprint.title: Wire Error Answer Reveal
slidesBlueprint.contentSummary: Duplicates the Spot-the-Error prompt and reveals the highlighted answer in place: Sam is wrong because 1 AND 1 produces 1 on intermediate wire P, and the NOT gate then inverts wire P from 1 to 0, leaving the final output bulb OFF (0).
slidesBlueprint.pupilActivity: Check your mini-whiteboard explanation against the revealed intermediate wire trace and correct any errors.

pedagogicalRationale.principle: Cognitive Load Theory: Immediate Feedback and Error Correction
pedagogicalRationale.cognitiveLoadNote: Pairs the hinge check with an immediate in-place reveal so no pupil carries the skipped-wire misconception into the 35-minute simulator workshop.

slidesBlueprint.title: Circuit Simulator Workshop
slidesBlueprint.contentSummary: Displays four progressive completed target truth tables (Challenge 1: 2-input NAND pattern 1, 1, 1, 0; Challenge 2: 2-input pattern 1, 1, 0, 1; Challenge 3: 3-input pattern combining AND into OR; Extension Challenge 4: 3-input multi-gate mystery table) alongside clear workshop steps: build a logic circuit in the online simulator for each target truth table, test every binary input row in ascending counting order to verify your outputs match, and draw the working circuit diagram with labelled intermediate wires into your book before advancing.
slidesBlueprint.pupilActivity: Construct and test logic circuits in the online simulator to match each completed target truth table, then copy each verified circuit diagram into your book.

pedagogicalRationale.principle: Rosenshine Principle 8: Provide Scaffolds for Difficult Tasks & Principle 9: Independent Practice
pedagogicalRationale.cognitiveLoadNote: Honours the teacher brief exception by dedicating the core workshop block to hands-on simulator construction while keeping target truth tables and book-recording instructions visible on screen.
pedagogicalRationale.retrievalLink: Applies ascending binary truth table rows (00, 01, 10, 11) from Lesson 4.

slidesBlueprint.title: Workshop Circuit Solutions
slidesBlueprint.contentSummary: Reveals the verified multi-gate circuit diagrams and intermediate wire columns (P) for Challenges 1 to 4 alongside their target truth tables so you can compare and self-mark the circuit diagrams drawn in your book.
slidesBlueprint.pupilActivity: Compare the circuit diagrams in your book against the revealed reference circuits, ticking each verified gate connection and intermediate wire label.

pedagogicalRationale.principle: Rosenshine Principle 7: Obtain a High Success Rate
pedagogicalRationale.cognitiveLoadNote: Provides immediate visual verification of the multi-gate topologies so pupils can confirm their recorded book diagrams are accurate.
pedagogicalRationale.retrievalLink: Consolidates truth table verification across multi-gate combinations.

slidesBlueprint.title: Reviewing Multi-Gate Logic Circuits
slidesBlueprint.contentSummary: Summarises today's three key takeaways in side-by-side cards: multi-gate circuits pass binary signals along intermediate wires from left to right; labelling intermediate wire states prevents tracing errors; testing every row in binary counting order proves a circuit matches its target truth table.
slidesBlueprint.pupilActivity: Read the three summary takeaways and reflect on how software simulators model the real transistor circuits inside a computer processor.

pedagogicalRationale.principle: Rosenshine Principle 10: Weekly and Monthly Review
pedagogicalRationale.cognitiveLoadNote: Consolidates procedural circuit construction into long-term schema and bridges toward physical silicon microchip fabrication in Lesson 6.
pedagogicalRationale.retrievalLink: Connects binary states (Lessons 1–3) and Boolean gates (Lessons 4–5) to physical hardware.

starterQuadrants.answer: 10001 (4-bit result 0001 with carry-out 1) — Yes, a 4-bit overflow error occurs.

starterQuadrants.imagePrompt: Clean black-and-white technical schematic symbol of a standard D-shaped 2-input AND logic gate with inputs A and B on the left and output on the right
starterQuadrants.question: Name the single logic gate shown in this diagram.
For an OR gate, when both inputs are true, will the output will be:
starterQuadrants.answer: A — True — The or gate turns on when at least one input is true

starterQuadrants.question: For an AND gate, when both inputs are true, will the output will be:
starterQuadrants.answer: A — True — The and gate turns on when both inputs are true

slidesData.speakerNotes: Give pupils 4 minutes to complete all four quadrants silently. Reveal each quadrant answer one at a time. In Q1, check that pupils wrote the carry row underneath and spotted the 5th bit overflowing the 4-bit nibble. In Q3, reinforce that Boolean OR is inclusive (1 OR 1 = 1).

customCanvasElements.content:
• A truth table lists every possible combination of OFF (0) and ON (1) inputs, each row is one combination.
• This truth table shows every input combination for the AND gate, When neither input is on, or only one input is on, the output stays off, only when both inputs are on does the truth table output an ON signal

slidesData.title: Chaining Gates With Wires

bodyBlocks.content:
We connect logic components (like inputs, outputs, and Gates) together using wires. A single logic gate on its own does not do much, logic gates are useful because we can connect any input to any output with wires, including connecting the output of one logic gate to the input of another
These logic gates are how actual computers work, the wires between logic gates is where the electricity for a computer is used, real logic gates are very small, as little as 500 atoms across, even a small computer like the IPhone 18 pro has more logic gates in it than there are people on the planet
